titre: Gluten, the Hunger Winter, and Willem Dicke's Five Children
accroche: They say the famine of 1944-1945 revealed gluten. Dicke was noting the role of bread as early as the 1930s: the bread drop was only a confirmation.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the version most often told, it is the winter of 1944-1945 that reveals the cause of celiac disease. The occupied Netherlands runs short of bread; the celiac children of the pediatrician Willem Dicke get better; when airplanes drop bread, they relapse. The historians Yan and Holt do report the bread drop and the relapse, but the order is inverted, and the essential lies elsewhere.

Celiac disease is a disorder of the small intestine that interferes with the absorption of food, fats in particular, what is called malabsorption. Its trigger is gluten, the set of proteins in wheat and a few other cereals, of which gliadin is a part.

## An Often Fatal Disease, Scattered Clues

Dicke finishes his medical studies in 1928. At the time, celiac disease often kills: according to the studies cited by Yan and Holt, short-term mortality runs from 10% to over 35%. In the 1930s, he questions parents about what worsens or relieves the symptoms, and bread and rusks keep coming up. In 1941, he publishes a short article on a simple diet: according to Yan and Holt, the reference diets of the time, based on bananas in particular, are then unworkable in the occupied Netherlands.

His observations therefore precede the famine by a decade. When bread is parachuted in and his patients quickly deteriorate, Dicke notes it, but the historians Yan and Holt describe the episode as one more confirmation, not as the origin of the idea.

## Five Children and a Measurement

After the war, Dicke moves from clinical impression to experiment. All of his initial studies concern five patients, followed in detail in 1947-1948. He concludes that wheat flour is harmful, whereas wheat starch is not.

So that the conclusion does not rest on a mere impression, he relies on the biochemist Jan van de Kamer. In 1948, van de Kamer defended a thesis on the quantitative measurement of fat in stools, then developed with Weijers a fat balance: malabsorption becomes a number. Dicke defends his thesis at Utrecht in 1950, on the harmful effect of certain cereals in celiac patients.

## From Flour to Gliadin

In 1953, Dicke, Weijers, and van de Kamer publish in *Acta Paediatrica* an article on the presence in wheat of a factor harmful to celiac patients. The same year, van de Kamer, Weijers, and Dicke examine the constituents of wheat involved. According to Yan and Holt, it is gliadin, a wheat protein, that is judged harmful there.

How many discoveries attributed to a catastrophe were already waiting, in a notebook, for it to come and confirm them?

repere.texte: All of Dicke's initial studies were conducted on five patients.
repere.source: Yan and Holt, Clinical and Translational Science, vol. 2, no. 6, 2009 (retranslated from the French; original wording not retrieved)

carte.punch: The Hunger Winter did not discover gluten. It confirmed what Dicke had observed before.
carte.idee: Legend has it that the famine of 1944-1945 revealed the cause of celiac disease. Willem Dicke was noting the role of bread as early as the 1930s, studied five children, and relied on a measurement of fat in stools. The bread drop only confirmed his observations.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: van de Kamer J. H., Weijers H. A., Dicke W. K., “Coeliac disease. IV. An investigation into the injurious constituents of wheat…”, Acta Paediatrica, 1953
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The second 1953 article, on the harmful constituents of wheat.

quiz.question: What allowed Dicke to establish, after the war, that it was wheat flour, not wheat starch, that harmed celiac children?
choix: Diets tested on five patients, varying wheat and wheat starch, with van de Kamer's fat measurement
Only the return of relapses when bread was parachuted in during the 1944-1945 famine
A clinical hunch of Dicke's, based on his experience with no measurement or patient followed
The banana-based diets already recommended to celiac children before the war
quiz.explication: Dicke tested, on five patients followed in 1947-1948, diets varying rye flour, wheat flour, wheat starch, rice flour, and corn starch, and measured the effect thanks to the fat balance developed by van de Kamer and Weijers. The bread drop during the famine was, according to Yan and Holt, only one more confirmation; banana-based diets were the prewar reference, unworkable in the occupied Netherlands.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Before the famine of 1944-1945, how had Dicke already spotted the role of bread in the 1930s?
choix: By questioning his patients' parents about what worsened or relieved the symptoms, bread and rusks often coming up
By systematically comparing, from 1930, wheat-based diets and banana-based diets in his patients
By following five children over several years with regular measurement of the fat in their stools
By receiving the results of a Danish study on gluten, published before his own medical degree
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In the 1930s, Dicke questioned parents about what worsened or relieved their children's symptoms, and bread and rusks kept coming up in their answers, well before the famine and the fat measurement.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the studies cited by Yan and Holt, what was the short-term mortality of celiac disease when Dicke finished his medical studies?
choix: Mortality close to zero, the disease then being judged benign
Mortality strictly below 5%, already judged worrying
Mortality ranging from 10% to over 35%, depending on the studies cited
Mortality above 80% in most reported cases
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The studies cited by Yan and Holt put the short-term mortality of celiac disease, at the time Dicke finishes his studies in 1928, between 10% and over 35%, far from trivial.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the biochemist Jan van de Kamer contribute to Dicke's work after the war?
choix: A 1950 thesis on the harmful effect of certain cereals in celiac patients, defended by Dicke himself
A quantitative measurement of fat in stools, then a balance developed with Weijers, making malabsorption measurable
The discovery of gliadin as the responsible protein, published alone in 1948
The banana-based diet used as the reference before the war in the Netherlands
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Van de Kamer defended in 1948 a thesis on the quantitative measurement of fat in stools, then developed with Weijers a fat balance that makes malabsorption measurable as a number.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the two articles published in 1953 by Dicke, Weijers, and van de Kamer in Acta Paediatrica show?
choix: That wheat starch is the constituent responsible for the symptoms in celiac patients
That the banana-based diet remains, after the war, the most effective treatment for celiac disease
That the famine of 1944-1945 is the only experimental proof of the role of wheat in celiac disease
That wheat contains a factor harmful to celiac patients, later identified as gliadin, a wheat protein
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The first 1953 article describes a harmful factor present in wheat, and the second identifies that factor as gliadin, a wheat protein, and not as starch, which Dicke judged not harmful.
